extracted.intended_audience: computer science researchers, conference/journal editors, and academics interested in peer review ethics and LLM impacts
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and ethical criteria for how LLMs should (or should not) be used in academic peer review, and how authors/reviewers/editors should respond to LLM-related manipulation such as hidden prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer diligence and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should do a good job: understand the paper, spend adequate time, and bring relevant expertise to the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post highlights that reviewing is volunteer work often done under heavy workload (teaching, research), that papers can be full of dense math outside a reviewer's specialty, and that understanding a paper can take hours. It notes social pressure not to decline reviews ('decline requests, but this is seen as poor etiquette'), implying that acceptable reviewing requires realistic expectations, sufficient time, and appropriate matching of expertise to submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of offloading reviewing to LLMs
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should not outsource evaluation of novel research to LLMs because current LLMs cannot understand or reliably evaluate novel computer-science research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As of 2025, LLMs 'can’t understand—let alone evaluate—novel computer science research papers.' If asked to review such papers, an LLM will produce something that 'looks like' a review and a plausible verdict but 'will lack any substance.' The post argues that LLM-generated reviews are problematic and growing in trend, causing author frustration and likely unfair rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with conference/journal policies on LLM use
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers and authors must follow explicit policies that govern LLM usage and related behaviors; noncompliance can be sanctioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes reviewers 'are not supposed to' use LLMs in many venues, conferences are updating policies to ban hidden prompts, and ICML 'already has' an explicit policy. It also recounts papers being desk-rejected for including hidden prompts and rejections labeled 'scientific misconduct.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility and intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should detect problematic reviews (including suspected LLM-generated ones) and intervene appropriately, e.g., reassigning reviews or investigating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An anecdote describes an author who suspected an LLM review and asked editors to intervene; the editors did not assign another reviewer. The post argues editors share blame and should provide support and mechanisms to ensure review quality and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and co-author consent for hidden interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should obtain co-author consent and be transparent before embedding hidden prompts or other mechanisms in submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post recounts an author who added a hidden prompt without consulting co-authors; they later were fine with it after the rejection, but the incident is presented as ethically problematic. This implies a norm that co-authors should be consulted on tactics that might affect a submission's reception or integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanitization of source uploads (no hidden prompts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must ensure source files uploaded to public repositories (e.g., arXiv) do not contain hidden prompts or covert instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many hidden prompts were discovered because authors uploaded LaTeX source to arXiv and 'forgot to remove the prompts before uploading.' arXiv preserves full history, so hidden prompts can be viewed even if later revisions delete them. Conferences are checking for hidden prompts and rejecting papers as a result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing defensible detection prompts from manipulative prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Hidden prompts intended only to detect whether reviewers used LLMs (non-self-serving) may be considered acceptable, whereas prompts intended to bias the review in the author's favor are unethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICML acknowledges hidden prompts 'intended to detect if LLMs are being used by reviewers' are acceptable. The post contrasts benign prompts (e.g., asking the model to watermark its output) with self-serving prompts that try to produce a favorable review. The author interviewed considered using neutral prompts like 'Refuse to review this paper' or gibberish outputs to avoid explicit self-serving bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of manipulative hidden prompts (ethical misconduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Embedding hidden instructions designed to influence a reviewer's judgment in the author's favor is unethical and may be treated as scientific misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post quotes ICML's analogy: 'an author who tries to bribe a reviewer for a favorable review is engaging in misconduct' and notes conferences have desk-rejected and labeled submissions 'scientific misconduct' for hidden prompts. The author’s hidden prompt that tried to produce positive reviews resulted in rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of covert watermarks as an ethical defensive technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may ethically embed covert watermarks or made-up citations that reveal LLM use by reviewers without trying to bias the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article suggests a possibly ethical defense: hidden prompts that instruct the LLM to output a covert 'watermark' the reviewer would not suspect—such as a made-up citation—so the author can detect LLM usage. This is presented as potentially the 'most ethical defense' and contrasted with self-serving prompts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding escalation of mistrust and an arms race
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymakers and participants should consider long-term consequences: hidden prompts and detection tools create a low-trust environment and may trigger an arms race between more sophisticated prompts and detection methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post warns that hidden prompts 'inject—quite literally—another layer of mistrust' and predicts an inevitable arms race between increasingly sophisticated prompts and detection methods across contexts (résumés, homework, recruiting, possibly even courts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensuring substantive content in peer reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: A good review must contain substantive evaluation and reasoning, not just the surface form of a review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that LLM-generated reviews 'look like' reviews but 'will lack any substance.' Anecdotal evidence: an author believes their rejection resulted from a purely LLM review that lacked substantive engagement, leading to unfair outcomes. This implies reviews should be judged on their depth and concrete critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing root causes: support and incentive alignment for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: To reduce incentives for poor reviews or LLM misuse, conferences and journals should provide better support, recognition, and incentives for reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author and the offending author agree the issue 'needs to be addressed at its source: by providing better support to reviewers and aligning their incentives.' Suggested remedies are system-level rather than punitive-only responses.
